learn: Scientists are curious. They ask questions about the world, like "Why is the sky blue?" or "Where do worms go when it rains?"
A good question is something we can try to find out by looking or testing.
Anyone can be a scientist. You just need to wonder and look closely.
check: Anyone who wonders and looks closely
Where do worms go when it rains?
lessons.try: Look out of a window and think of one question about what you see.

learn: We learn about the world with our five senses.
We see with our eyes, hear with our ears, smell with our nose, taste with our tongue and touch with our skin.
Scientists use their senses to observe. To observe means to look very carefully and notice details.
check: How many senses do we have?
lessons.try: Hold a leaf. Say what you see, feel and smell.

learn: Scientists stay safe. We only taste things a grown-up says are safe to eat.
We wash our hands after touching soil, animals or plants.
We never put things in our ears, nose or mouth during science, and we ask a grown-up for help.
check: When can we taste something in science?
Only when a grown-up says it is safe
What should we do after touching soil?
Who should we ask for help?
lessons.try: Tell a grown-up two safety rules for science time.

learn: A push moves something away from you. A pull moves something toward you.
Pushes and pulls are called forces.
Opening a door can be a push or a pull. Kicking a ball is a push. Pulling a wagon is a pull.
lessons.try: Find three things at home you push and three things you pull.

learn: A force can make something start moving. A push starts a toy car rolling.
A force can make something stop. Your hand stops a rolling ball.
A force can change direction. A kick can send a ball a new way.
check: What can make a toy car start moving?
What happens when your hand catches a rolling ball?
A force can change a ball's...
lessons.try: Roll a ball, stop it with your hand, then push it a new way.

learn: A bigger push makes something move faster or farther.
A small push makes it move only a little.
When two things bump, they push on each other and can change how they move.
check: A big push makes a ball go...
A small push makes something move...
lessons.try: Push a ball gently, then harder. Which went farther?

learn: Living things grow and change. They need food or energy, water and air.
Living things can make more of their own kind. Cats have kittens. Plants make seeds.
People, animals and plants are all living things.
lessons.try: Name three living things you can see right now.

learn: Nonliving things do not eat, drink, breathe or grow by themselves.
Rocks, toys, chairs and water are nonliving.
A toy robot may move, but it does not eat or grow, so it is not alive.
check: Is a rock living or nonliving?
A toy robot moves. Is it alive?
No, it does not eat or grow
lessons.try: Sort pictures into living and nonliving.

learn: Some things were once alive. A dry leaf was part of a living tree.
Wood came from a tree. A shell was once the home of a living animal.
Scientists look closely to decide if something is living, nonliving or was once alive.
check: The home of a living animal
lessons.try: Find something that was once alive, like a leaf or a stick.

learn: Plants are living things. They need sunlight, water and air to grow.
Many plants also grow in soil, which holds them up and gives them water.
A plant with no water wilts and droops. Water helps it stand tall again.
check: What happens to a plant with no water?
What does soil do for many plants?
Holds them up and gives water
lessons.try: Water a plant and watch how it looks over a few days.

learn: Plants make their own food. They use sunlight to do it.
That is why plants grow toward the light. A plant on a windowsill bends to the window.
Animals cannot make their own food this way. They need to eat.
check: What do plants use to make food?
A plant on a windowsill bends toward...
Can animals make food from sunlight like plants?
lessons.try: Put a plant by a window. Turn it after a week and watch it bend back.

learn: Roots take in water from the soil and hold the plant in place.
The stem holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves.
Leaves catch the sunlight to make food.
check: Which part takes in water from the soil?
Holds the plant up and carries water
lessons.try: Draw a plant and label the roots, stem and leaves.

learn: Animals need food, water, air and a safe place to live called a shelter.
A bird builds a nest. A rabbit digs a burrow. A bear rests in a den.
Animals cannot make their own food, so they must find it.
check: Where does a bird often live?
Can animals make their own food?
lessons.try: Name an animal and its shelter.

learn: Some animals eat plants, like cows, rabbits and deer.
Some animals eat other animals, like lions and owls.
Some eat both plants and animals, like bears and people.
lessons.try: Sort animals into plant eaters, meat eaters and both.

learn: Pets are animals that live with people. They need care every day.
A pet needs fresh water, the right food, a clean home and gentle love.
Some animals are wild. We watch wild animals from a distance and do not touch them.
check: What does a pet need every day?
Fresh water and the right food
What should we do with wild animals?
lessons.try: Make a list of what a dog or cat needs each day.

units.t: Plants and Animals Change Their World

learn: Living things change the places they live.
A squirrel digs holes to hide nuts. Some nuts it forgets grow into new trees.
Beavers cut trees with their teeth and build dams across streams. The dam makes a pond.
check: What can a forgotten nut become?
lessons.try: Look outside for signs that an animal changed something: holes, nests or tracks.

learn: Plant roots can grow into cracks and break rocks or sidewalks.
Trees give shade and homes to birds and insects.
Fallen leaves rot and make the soil rich for new plants.
check: What can roots do to a sidewalk?
Fallen leaves help make the soil...
lessons.try: Find a crack in a sidewalk with a plant growing in it.

learn: People change the land too. We build roads, houses and farms.
Some changes can hurt plants and animals, like litter and dirty water.
People can also help: plant trees, pick up trash and make parks.
check: How can people help the land?
Plant trees and pick up trash
lessons.try: Think of one way you can help the land near your home.

learn: The sun is a star. It is very far away and very big.
The sun gives us light and heat.
Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes.
check: What does the sun give us?
Is it safe to look straight at the sun?
lessons.try: Feel a window on a sunny day. Is it warm?

learn: Sunlight warms the land, water and air.
A sidewalk in the sun feels hotter than one in the shade.
Shade is a place where something blocks the sunlight, like a tree or an umbrella.
check: Which feels hotter on a sunny day?
lessons.try: Touch a sunny spot and a shady spot outside. Which is warmer?

learn: We can stay cool in the shade on a hot day.
Hats, sunglasses and sunscreen protect us from too much sun.
People build roofs and plant trees to make shade.
check: What protects your skin from the sun?
Where can we stay cool on a hot day?
Why do people plant trees near houses?
lessons.try: Design a shade for a toy using paper and sticks.

learn: Weather is what the air outside is like right now.
It can be sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy or snowy.
We look out of the window and feel the air to tell the weather.
check: What the air outside is like right now
Which is a kind of weather?
How can we tell the weather?
Look outside and feel the air
lessons.try: Look outside and say today's weather.

learn: A thermometer tells how hot or cold it is.
A rain gauge catches rain to show how much fell.
Scientists who study weather are called meteorologists.
check: What tells how hot or cold it is?
What catches rain to measure it?
lessons.try: Put a cup outside on a rainy day. How much rain did it catch?

learn: Weather changes from day to day.
We can keep a weather chart and look for patterns, like more rainy days in spring.
Weather helps us choose what to wear: a coat for cold, a hat for sun, boots for rain.
check: Does weather change from day to day?
What should you wear on a rainy day?
What can a weather chart show?
lessons.try: Keep a weather chart for one week.

learn: There are four seasons: spring, summer, fall and winter.
They come in the same order every year.
In many places summer is warm, winter is cold, and spring and fall are in between.
lessons.try: Draw a tree in each of the four seasons.

learn: In spring, many plants grow new leaves and flowers.
In fall, leaves change colour and drop in many places.
Some animals sleep through winter, and some birds fly to warmer places.
check: When do many plants grow new flowers?
When do leaves change colour and drop?
What do some birds do in winter?
lessons.try: Name one thing that happens in fall.

learn: Some weather is dangerous: thunderstorms, tornadoes, hurricanes and blizzards.
Weather forecasters warn people so they can get ready.
In a storm, stay inside with a grown-up, away from windows. When thunder roars, go indoors.
lessons.try: Make a storm safety plan with a grown-up.

learn: Living things need clean air, clean water and land.
Reduce means using less. Turn off the water while you brush your teeth.
Turn off lights when you leave a room to save energy.
check: Turn it off while brushing teeth
What should you do when leaving a room?
lessons.try: Find two ways your family can use less water or electricity.

learn: Reuse means using something again.
A jar can hold crayons. A box can become a toy house.
Fixing a toy instead of throwing it away is reusing too.
check: How can a jar be reused?
lessons.try: Make something new from an old box or jar.

learn: Recycle means making old things into new things.
Paper, cans and some plastic can be recycled.
We put them in the recycling bin so a factory can make them into new things.
check: Making old things into new things
lessons.try: Sort clean trash into recycling and not recycling.
